title: What Is the Best Payment Solution for ISVs?
summary: Looking for the best payment solution for ISVs? Explore key features, costs, integrations, and long-term benefits.
body_markdown:
Choosing a payment solution should be easy.


Accept money. Move money. Reconcile money. Go home at a reasonable hour.


Instead, many independent software vendors find themselves evaluating payment gateways, merchant acquirers, payment facilitators, sponsor banks, card networks, risk providers, payout companies, compliance tools, and reporting systems. By the end of the process, the payment diagram looks less like financial infrastructure and more like someone dropped a plate of spaghetti on a whiteboard.


The best payment solution for an ISV does more than process transactions. It fits the ISV’s business model, improves the customer experience, supports future growth, reduces operational complexity, and creates economic value.


For many U.S.-focused ISVs, the right solution combines embedded payment acceptance, automated merchant onboarding, recurring billing, reporting, reconciliation, revenue sharing, and funds disbursement through one relationship.


That is a long sentence. Unfortunately, payments are not famous for brevity.


## What Should ISVs Look for in a Payment Solution?


An ISV should evaluate every payment partner across five essential areas:


1. Integration and implementation


2. Customer experience


3. Payment monetization


4. Risk and compliance support


5. Long-term product flexibility


Price matters, of course. However, selecting a payment processor based only on the lowest quoted rate is like choosing a restaurant because it has the cheapest napkins. It sounds financially responsible until dinner arrives.


The real cost of a payment platform includes development time, onboarding friction, support demands, administrative work, failed transactions, reconciliation problems, compliance responsibilities, and lost revenue opportunities.


A provider offering a slightly lower processing rate often costs more when the ISV must add separate vendors for merchant onboarding, disbursements, card issuing, reporting, customer communications, or printed checks.


The best payment partner solves more problems than it creates.


## Why Do Embedded Payments Matter for ISVs?


[Embedded payments](https://usio.com/embedded-payments/) allow customers to complete financial transactions inside the software they already use. Customers stay within the application instead of opening a separate portal, creating another account, or landing on a checkout page that looks as though it survived the dial-up era.


A unified experience strengthens the product and gives the ISV greater control over how payments fit into the customer journey.


Payments also become part of the software’s value proposition, retention strategy, operating model, and revenue engine. Instead of handing the customer relationship to a third-party processor, the ISV delivers a consistent experience from the original workflow through the final transaction.


Research supports the broader economic importance of digital payments. A Bank for International Settlements study covering 101 economies found that a one-percentage-point increase in digital payment use was associated with a 0.10-percentage-point increase in gross domestic product per capita growth over two years. The researchers also linked digital payment use to greater financial inclusion and credit access.


[\[bis.org\]](https://www.bis.org/publications/working-paper-1196-digital-payments-informality-and-economic-growth.pdf)


For an ISV, embedded payments do not simply add a “Pay Now” button. They make the software more useful, expand its role in the customer’s operations, and create a stronger reason for customers to stay.


## How Does Payment Choice Affect the Customer Experience?


Customers do not all want to pay the same way. That would be wonderfully convenient for finance teams, but consumers have stubbornly chosen to remain individuals.


Federal Reserve research found that consumers respond strongly to the time required at checkout and to whether a payment method draws from available liquidity or debt. Convenience and financial context influence how people choose to pay.


[\[federalreserve.gov\]](https://www.federalreserve.gov/pubs/feds/2006/200617/200617pap.pdf)


ISVs should therefore build payment options around the customer’s actual workflow.


Depending on the industry and customer base, those options could include:


- Credit and debit cards


- Bank-account payments


- Recurring payments


- [Hosted payment pages](https://usio.com/hosted-payment-pages-a-smarter-way-to-accept-payments/)
- Digital wallets


- Card-present transactions


- Real-time payments


- Refunds and outbound disbursements


- Printed checks for recipients who still enjoy opening envelopes


The strongest solution does not offer every payment method merely for brochure decoration. It provides the methods customers use today and gives the ISV room to add more as its product grows.


## How Will Payments Generate Revenue for an ISV?


Payments become a recurring revenue source when the ISV participates in transaction economics.


Under a traditional processing arrangement, the ISV integrates a payment provider because customers need a way to pay. The processor earns the payment revenue, while the ISV inherits the technical questions, support requests, and customer complaints.


It is like hosting a party, cleaning the house, buying the snacks, and then letting someone else charge admission.


A


[payment-facilitation](https://usio.com/embedded-payments-vs-payment-facilitation-for-platforms/) model changes that equation. The right arrangement gives the ISV more control over the payment experience, merchant pricing, customer onboarding, and transaction revenue.


Before counting that revenue, the ISV should ask:


- Does revenue sharing begin at launch or only after a volume threshold?


- Who controls merchant pricing?


- Which expenses come out before the provider calculates the revenue split?


- How frequently does the provider pay revenue?


- Does the ISV receive transparent transaction and revenue reporting?


- Does the agreement include minimums or exclusivity requirements?


- How does the revenue model change as transaction volume increases?


- Who owns the merchant relationship?


A revenue-sharing percentage sounds impressive until nobody can explain the number it multiplies.


The right payment relationship turns transaction volume into an additional revenue stream. The wrong one gives the ISV more work and sends the economics somewhere else.


## Should an ISV Become a Payment Facilitator?


Becoming a registered payment facilitator gives a software company greater control, but it also introduces underwriting, compliance, merchant monitoring, fraud management, financial risk, sponsor-bank oversight, and substantial operational responsibilities.


That structure fits large platforms that treat payments as a core business and build the teams required to manage it. It rarely fits an ISV that wants to focus on creating excellent software for healthcare practices, nonprofit organizations, insurance companies, property managers, government agencies, fitness studios, lenders, or other specialized markets.


[Payment-facilitation-as-a-service](https://usio.com/usio-payment-facilitation/) offers a more practical alternative. The ISV embeds a branded payment experience and participates in payment economics while the payment partner handles more of the underlying infrastructure, underwriting, compliance, and risk management.


No reputable provider owns a magic “make compliance disappear” wand. If one claims otherwise, keep one hand on your wallet and the other on the exit door.


A strong partnership clearly divides responsibilities. The ISV knows what it owns, what the payment provider owns, and who responds when something goes wrong.


## Why Do Merchant Onboarding and Customer Support Matter?


A successful integration only marks the beginning. After launch, downstream businesses must enroll, verify their information, receive approval, activate their accounts, and learn how to use the payment service.


Slow or confusing onboarding kills adoption. The ISV builds a beautiful payment feature, but customers never activate it. This is the software equivalent of constructing a luxury swimming pool and forgetting the water.


ISVs should ask:


- Does merchant onboarding take place inside the software?


- Which business and ownership information must merchants provide?


- How does the provider handle underwriting exceptions?


- How quickly do applicants receive decisions?


- Does the onboarding experience reflect the ISV’s brand?


- Who assists a merchant when an application stalls?


- Does the ISV see each application’s status?


- How does the provider communicate ongoing risk reviews?


Support deserves equal scrutiny. A payment company might operate impressive technology and still create a miserable partnership if every question disappears into a ticket queue.


Payment problems rarely arrive politely during a scheduled quarterly review. They tend to appear at 4:57 p.m. on Friday with a subject line containing “URGENT,” “DECLINING,” and several punctuation marks.


## Does the Payment Provider Support Money In and Money Out?


Many payment providers focus primarily on collecting money. ISVs increasingly need infrastructure that also sends money out.


A software platform might need to:


- Refund a patient or customer


- Pay a contractor


- Distribute an insurance claim


- Return a security deposit


- Send financial assistance


- Pay a marketplace seller


- Issue an incentive or rebate


- Send money to a bank account or debit card


- Create a physical or virtual card


- Print and mail a check


Separate providers for payment acceptance, disbursements, card programs, and printed payments create more integrations, fragmented reporting, and additional vendor relationships. They also force the ISV to determine which provider owns the problem when a transaction fails.


Spoiler: every provider initially suspects another provider.


A unified money-movement platform connects incoming and outgoing transactions within a broader financial workflow.


For vertical ISVs, that reach matters. A property-management platform collects rent and returns deposits. An insurance platform accepts premiums and distributes claims. A healthcare platform collects patient balances and issues refunds. A nonprofit platform accepts donations and distributes financial assistance.


Money rarely travels in only one direction. An ISV should choose a partner that understands the entire journey.


## Does an ISV Need a Global Payment Platform?


If more than 50% of your payment activity occurs in the United States, consider making a U.S.-focused payment partner the foundation of your payment strategy.


Why pay for extensive international infrastructure, currency-conversion capabilities, regional payment methods, and cross-border functionality when most of your customers will never use them?


That is like buying an international roaming plan when most of your calls happen inside your office.


Global payment platforms make sense when an ISV processes meaningful transaction volume across several countries and currencies. If most merchants, customers, and transactions operate in the United States, a U.S.-focused provider often delivers a better match between the services the business needs and the services it pays for.


Before selecting a global platform, ask:


- What percentage of our payment volume occurs outside the United States?


- How many currencies do we need to support today?


- Which international markets already produce meaningful revenue?


- Do our customers require local international payment methods?


- What will we pay for cross-border processing and currency conversion?


- Does the provider support the U.S. payment methods our users need?


- Are we choosing the platform for our current business or for an expansion plan that might never materialize?


The 50% threshold serves as a practical evaluation point, not a universal law. Every ISV should review its actual transaction volume, markets, currencies, and product roadmap.


Global reach delivers real value when the business needs it. When the business does not, it becomes an expensive collection of flags on a sales presentation.

An ISV does not need to route every transaction through one global provider simply because it serves international customers.


If your software requires strong U.S. payment capabilities and international reach, consider a payment stack that combines


**Usio for U.S. payment activity with Stripe for international transactions** .


Stripe supports charges in more than 135 currencies, which makes it a logical option for platforms that need broad international coverage. Usio serves as the U.S. money-movement partner, supporting domestic payment acceptance and broader financial workflows.


[\[docs.stripe.com\]](https://docs.stripe.com/currencies)


This payment stack gives an ISV:


- A partner aligned with its core U.S. transaction volume


- International currency support where the business actually needs it


- More flexibility than forcing every transaction through one provider

- A path toward international expansion without overbuilding the U.S. payment experience


The ISV must design the architecture intentionally. The team should define which transactions go through Usio, which transactions go through Stripe, and how the software handles transaction routing, reporting, reconciliation, and customer support.


A two-provider strategy should never become a payment scavenger hunt in which customers and employees guess which company handled a transaction.


The strategy works because each company fills a specific role.


**Use Usio where your U.S. payment requirements run deepest. Use Stripe where international reach becomes essential. Together, they create a payment stack that fits your business rather than forcing your business to fit one provider.**


Global when you need it. U.S.-focused where it matters. Not every transaction needs to carry a passport.


## How Should ISVs Compare Payment Providers?


ISVs should score providers against the actual requirements of their software instead of relying on a generic feature checklist.


**Integration**


- Does the integration fit the ISV’s development resources?


- Does the provider offer hosted, embedded, or customized options?


- Can the ISV add payment functions in phases?


- Does the provider offer testing tools and technical support?


**Economics**


- Will the ISV participate in payment revenue?


- Does the provider explain its pricing clearly?


- Will the ISV pay setup, platform, integration, or per-merchant charges?


- Which transaction assumptions support the quoted pricing?


**Customer experience**


- Will the payment experience stay under the ISV’s brand?


- Does the provider simplify merchant onboarding?


- Does the platform support recurring payments and stored payment methods?


- Will customers receive the payment choices appropriate for the industry?


**Operations**


- How does the provider handle refunds, disputes, chargebacks, and failed payments?


- Will reporting support accurate reconciliation?


- Does the ISV receive visibility into merchant and transaction status?


- Does the provider offer a clear escalation process?


**Future expansion**


- Does the provider support outbound disbursements?


- Does it offer physical or virtual card programs?


- Does it support electronic billing or printed communications?


- Will the ISV need another vendor when its product roadmap expands?


- Can the ISV add international coverage without replacing its U.S. payment infrastructure?


The final category often determines the long-term value of the partnership. A provider that meets today’s requirements but blocks tomorrow’s roadmap will eventually become the most expensive option, even when its initial proposal looks inexpensive.


## What Is the Best Payment Solution for U.S.-Based ISVs?


No provider wins every use case.


A global marketplace operating in dozens of currencies has different payment requirements from a U.S.-based healthcare, government, nonprofit, insurance, property-management, or business-software platform.


For U.S.-focused ISVs seeking embedded payment acceptance, automated merchant onboarding, payment monetization, disbursements, card issuing, bank-account payments, real-time payment options, and print-and-mail capabilities, Usio deserves serious consideration.


Usio fits ISVs that want to:


- Keep the payment experience under their own brand


- Generate recurring transaction revenue


- Avoid building a payment-facilitation operation from scratch


- Support incoming and outgoing payments


- Reduce the number of payment vendors they manage


- Access direct implementation and operational support


- Expand into additional money-movement services


The value goes beyond processing transactions. Plenty of companies process payments.


Usio supports more of the financial lifecycle surrounding the software. If international currencies also matter, Usio will anchor the U.S. payment strategy while Stripe supports broader global requirements.


## Which Payment Platform Should an ISV Choose?


The best payment solution for an ISV accomplishes four things:


1. It makes payments easier for the software’s users.


2. It creates sustainable economics for the ISV.


3. It reduces operational and technical complexity.


4. It supports where the product is going, not just where it stands today.


For many U.S.-based ISVs, that means looking beyond a basic gateway or card processor. It means choosing an embedded money-movement platform that connects acceptance, onboarding, reporting, monetization, and disbursements within one strategy.


If more than 50% of your payment needs occur in the United States, do not assume a global provider automatically delivers greater value. A provider that specializes in U.S. payments will focus your investment on the capabilities your customers actually use instead of bundling your strategy around international currency infrastructure you rarely need.


If global coverage remains essential, you do not have to sacrifice the advantages of a U.S.-focused provider. A payment stack combining Usio and Stripe delivers domestic specialization and international reach.


The best payment platform does not simply help an ISV collect money. It helps the ISV build a better product, strengthen customer relationships, generate recurring revenue, and move money wherever the business workflow requires.


Preferably without turning the software team into amateur payment archaeologists.
